description: Seen at the end of the road.  Has been here forever.  Probably Quercus x schuettei.  Originally identified as a Bur Oak since the leaves had more macrocarpa characteristics and the acorns seen many years ago were macrocarpa like, but the leaves don't match either typical macrocarpa or bicolor. It rarely fruits, but this year did find two acorns, both in between bicolor and macrocarpa, so thinking this is a hybrid since Quercus regularly hybridize.  There were large bicolors in the area many years ago, but not many left now.  Don't know if any macrocarpas are around, but very well could be or could've been (most likely).  Didn't find any in my inventory of trees in the village back in the 90's.  Gorgeous tree either way.  As of the early '90's the circumference was 12' 3.5", diameter is 3' 11".  Haven't done the height yet or spread.  A remenant of the forest that used to be here.

description:
Tentatively sharing this as wild.

Small tree, no more than 20 years old, by artificial pond on the edges of a large lawn along woodland border.

If the tree had been a common oak, I would have presumed this was growing wild. However, cherrybark oak are rare in the region and not known from Randolph County, so I was suspicious.

I had always suspected that should there be cherrybark oak in Randolph County, then I would likely find them near the Tallapoosa River below the RL Harris Dam, and that's exactly where I found this tree. The pond nearby was formed by daming a creek that fed into the Tallapoosa.

The homeowner is an elderly widow who has lived there for decades. She claims that the only trees planted by pond were 2 weeping willows, and that she believes the cherrybark oak to be growing wild. If it was planted, she doesn't remember it being so.

Unfortunately, I was unable to see any other cherrybark oak in the area, although I was unable to do more than a cursory search. I would like to return and see if more trees can be located.

description:
"One of these things is not like the other" 

I was walking around Summit Park today. Almost all of the native trees here (let alone the oaks) are valley oaks, but up on the hill from the path nearby, I saw one large, slightly bushier oak with seemingly more pastel-colored leaves. I realized after taking a closer look that it appears to be a blue oak. It looks very old based on the trunk size (>a century old). I could not find any acorns on it, but that was also true for the valley oaks nearby for the most part (too many acorn-eating animals nearby)

Several valley oaks of various sizes and ages with lots of young seedlings underneath (<2 yrs old). Pictured in focus is a large, mature specimen. 

Seedling: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/258212479

Young tree: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/258212484

Almost all of the oaks here (in the woodlands) are blue oaks, Tucker's oaks, and their hybrids (Alvord's oaks). There are also some California scrub oaks in the chaparral regions nearby. 

Honestly, the lobing makes me think that this has Q. lobata in it as well (all of the surrounding oaks are seemingly Q. john-tuckeri, Q. douglasii, hybrids of the former, and Q. berberidifolia, but Q. lobata is found less than a mile away), but the other traits and surrounding environment are all suggestive of Alvord's oak imo.

*Quercus marilandica × velutina*.

Both parents nearby.

Leaves broadest toward the tip, distinctly but shallowly lobed. Petioles shorter than *Q. velutina*, but also longer than *Q. marilandica*. Twigs more pubescent than *Q. velutina*, but less so than *Q. marilandica*. Bark of lower trunk resembling *Q. marilandica*, but upper trunk similar to *Q. velutina*. The acorns of *Q. marilandica* and *Q. velutina* are quite similar, and so here too are the acorns of this tree. This eliminates scarlet oak, *Quercus coccinea*, as a possible parent in favor of black oak, because scarlet oak parentage could be expected to produce larger and wider acorns.

description: Tentatively *Quercus coccinea* × *velutina*. Based on the original description and images published by Kendell Laughlin in 1968, I suspect this tree might be a coclut oak. Both proposed parents species are nearby. The bark of the lower trunk resembles the dark furrows of black oak, but the bark of the upper trunk is noticeably thin and pale, merely fissured, more resembling scarlet oak. The leaves of the upper canopy resemble scarlet oak but more reliably 7-lobed and with U-shaped rather than C-shaped sinuses. The leaves of the lower canopy more resemble black oak, though somewhat diminished in size. Laughlin specifically mentions the asymmetrical leaf bases, and that character is evident on many of the leaves. The leaf pubescence is closer to black oak, clustered in the vein axes but also spread over the whole leaf blade. The upper canopy leaves are more sparsely hairy than the lower canopy leaves. Buds and twigs are plausibly intermediate. Acorns appear to favor black oak, but Laughlin also mentions this possibility in his original description. Difficult tree to judge, but it definitely struck me as odd when first looking up at the canopy and then also noticing the bark. Check out the last image for an impression of what that looked like. Note: It appears that some online sources, including iNaturalist, have given this species the common name "Fontana's oak". This is presumably a lazy analogy to other hybrid oaks which are frequently named to honor someone. In this instance, "fontana" is simply latin for "fountain". There is no person called Fontana who this hybrid oak is named for. The original common name bestowed upon this species by its discoverers was the rather clumsy "coclut oak", derived from "COCcinea" and "veLUTina". I added that as a regional name for North America, but the default name elsewhere remains Fontana's oak.

Quercus (Oak) are in the Beech (Fagaceae) family.
Those found in Monterey County are in three groups: Red (or Black) Oaks, Intermediate Oaks, and White Oaks. Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks have acorns that generally mature over a 2 year period (Coast Live Oak is an exception to this rule). White Oaks have acorns that mature in a single season. Most Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks are evergreen (California Black Oak being the exception). White Oaks may be either evergreen or deciduous. Hybrid forms are common. All oaks are monoecious, with conspicuous male flowers. Female flowers are found in the axils of the leaves near the tips of the new stems.

description:
Canyon Live Oak with many acorns at this time of year, both on the tree, and on the ground.

Canyon Live Oak (Quercus chrysolepis), a.k.a. Canyon Oak, Golden Cup Oak or Maul Oak is a native, evergreen tree in the Beech (Fagaceae) family that grows in canyons and on slopes in many plant communities, including near the coast and in the desert. It is the most widely distributed Oak in California. Leaves are flat, not cupped, leathery, oblong to oblong- or round-ovate, adaxially (top-side) dark green, abaxially (underside) golden or pale, puberulent when young, and glabrous in age. Leaf tips are acute to abruptly pointed. Margins are variable and can be entire, or spine-toothed. Acorns are oblong, ovoid, or elliptic. The cup is more distinctive. It is shallow with thick, sometimes tubercled scales and is covered with golden hairs when young. Peak bloom time: April-May. Peak flowering time: April-May.

OAKs (genus Quercus) in general, have a worldwide distribution in Mediterranean climates.

Quercus (Oak) are in the Beech (Fagaceae) family.
Those found in Monterey County are in three groups: Red (or Black) Oaks, Intermediate Oaks, and White Oaks. Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks have acorns that generally mature over a 2 year period (Coast Live Oak is an exception to this rule). White Oaks have acorns that mature in a single season. Most Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks are evergreen (California Black Oak being the exception). White Oaks may be either evergreen or deciduous. Hybrid forms are common. All oaks are monoecious, with conspicuous male flowers. Female flowers are found in the axils of the leaves near the tips of the new stems.

description: Found within a patch of chaparral with some Q. corneleus-mulleri, some Q. berberidifolia (presumably), and some hybrids with more Q. engelmani characteristics (taller, longer leaves, but still not distinctly Engelman).

Another interesting white scrub oak. Undersized acorn caps, and acorns with rather acute tips. More blue-hued but more squat leaves overall compared to many of the other scrub oaks in the area that had more elongate leaves. I've become rather curious about where the more rounded leaf charateristics come from seeing as how many of the type-species descriptions for San Diego white oaks have rather long leaves. Though I didn't get any photos f the entire plant, it stood roughly 6' tall and had a shrub habit.

Interesting individual showing semi-deciduous characteristics, reddish caps, generally entire leaves, many with pointed tips, and acorns with highly acute tips. I would think the deciduous nature was inherited from Engelman along with some of the leaf characteristics. The emerald-hue of the leaves has me suspicious of the remaining parentage as Q. berberidifolia-like individuals were also fairly common in the area. The acute tips of the acorn seem more reminiscent of Q. cornelius-mulleri which were also present nearby. No pure Q. engelmanii were found in the area, but some were certainly leaning towards Engelman.

Muller's Oak (Quercus cornelius-mulleri) A.k.a. Desert Scrub Oak. Formerly called Quercus dumosa. Native oak that grows up to 3 meters (10 feet) tall. It is a bushy, shrubby, and densely branched with tangled twigs. Leaves are evergreen, leathery and thick, oblong, ovate, or narrowly obovate with margins entire or 4--6-toothed. Leaves are adaxially (upper surface) sparsely puberulent and abaxially (underside) whitish and densely fine-tomentose. Habitat is chaparral and pinyon woodland, generally growing in granitic soils. Muller's oak was segregated from the Quercus dumosa complex in 1981 and was found to warrant species status of its own.

Quercus (Oak) are in the Beech (Fagaceae) family. Oaks in general, have a worldwide distribution in Mediterranean climates.
Those found in Monterey County, CA are in three groups: Red (or Black) Oaks, Intermediate Oaks, and White Oaks. Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks have acorns that generally mature over a 2 year period (Coast Live Oak is an exception to this rule). White Oaks have acorns that mature in a single season. Most Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks are evergreen (California Black Oak being the exception). White Oaks may be either evergreen or deciduous. Hybrid forms are common. All oaks are monoecious, with conspicuous male flowers. Female flowers are found in the axils of the leaves near the tips of the new stems.

Muller's Oak (Quercus cornelius-mulleri) A.k.a. Desert Scrub Oak. Formerly called Quercus dumosa. Native oak that grows up to 3 meters (10 feet) tall. It is a bushy, shrubby, and densely branched with tangled twigs. Leaves are evergreen, leathery and thick, oblong, ovate, or narrowly obovate with margins entire or 4--6-toothed. Leaves are adaxially (upper surface) sparsely puberulent and abaxially (underside) whitish and densely fine-tomentose. Habitat is chaparral and pinyon woodland, generally growing in granitic soils. Muller's oak was segregated from the Quercus dumosa complex in 1981 and was found to warrant species status of its own.

Quercus (Oak) are in the Beech (Fagaceae) family. Oaks in general, have a worldwide distribution in Mediterranean climates.
Those found in Monterey County, CA are in three groups: Red (or Black) Oaks, Intermediate Oaks, and White Oaks. Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks have acorns that generally mature over a 2 year period (Coast Live Oak is an exception to this rule). White Oaks have acorns that mature in a single season. Most Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks are evergreen (California Black Oak being the exception). White Oaks may be either evergreen or deciduous. Hybrid forms are common. All oaks are monoecious, with conspicuous male flowers. Female flowers are found in the axils of the leaves near the tips of the new stems.

"Plant galls are abnormal growths of plant tissues, similar to tumors or warts in animals, that have an external cause--such as an insect, mite, nematode, virus, fungus, bacterium, or even another plant species. Growths caused by genetic mutations are not galls. Nor are lerps and other constructions on a plant that do not contain plant tissue. "The 25,500-acre Pioneertown Mountains Preserve descends from the high piney 7,800-foot ridges into the Pioneertown Valley. The small community of Pioneertown is surrounded by conservancy-owned volcanic mesas, the Sawtooth Mountains, and preserve lands leading to the San Bernardino National Forest. The preserve has year-round riparian corridors in Pipes Canyon and Little Morongo Canyon. It is an important landscape linkage between Joshua Tree National Park, San Bernardino National Forest, and the Big Horn Mountains Bureau of Land Management Wilderness.
In 2006, the vast majority of the Joshua trees, pinyon pines and junipers at Pioneertown Mountains Preserve were killed in a 70,000-acre lightning-caused fire of unprecedented magnitude. Today, much of the preserve is going through natural vegetation succession. Some scientists predict that fire succession and climate change will favor scrub oak and Joshua tree plant communities that may replace the pinyon forests. The fire laid bare the region’s rich geological backbone."

description:
Mostly leafless, but definitely not lifeless!

Found a grove of shin oaks located on a somewhat steep, grassy slope with California interior chaparral (Q. berberidifolia, Q. wislizeni frutescens, Cercocarpus betuloides, California buckwheat, chamise, etc.) on either side along the trail (facing south). The trail in question is one of the routes (the most diagonal one) from Bouquet Canyon Road at Lincoln Crest up Mount McDill. 

At the first opening of the chaparral southward and upward on the trail, shin oaks can be seen dotting the landscape in the hills further up, e.g., I saw some trees with orange-yellow leaves throughout the hills or obvious oaks with no leaves along the ridge at the top. It appears that shin oaks grow at higher elevations, not only because they probably can better handle colder weather and harsher winds/frost, but also because they cannot compete with the interior chaparral in the rockier, iron-rich serpentine soil at lower elevations. 

Photos of buds, leaves (rotted/fallen, dead ones still on the trees, and new growth), bark, acorn caps, growth habit, and surrounding environment.

description: In a large, mature, mostly publicly owned forest tract on a gradual north-facing slope, dominated by red oak and red maple, uncommon for Worcester County. Mature, tall white pine occurs  in small patches mostly on the east side, where 200 year old stone walls are prominent, some of which are double wide indicating formerly plowed fields and the presence of deeper, richer soil. An additional feature is the complete absence of woody invasive species. Mountain laurel and witch hazel are uncommon, in contrast to much of the surrounding area forests. White birch is more common than black birch, another unusual feature. White ash is occasional, some have been attacked by emerald ash borer and are dying out. Hemlock is occasional and no longer casting a deep shade, having been affected by hemlock wooly adelgid. Since I had a metric diameter tape handy, I decided to use it, both to give a more accurate sense of this stand, and to allow future biologists to directly compare. Tape shows diameter in centimeters and millimeters, to which I will add inches in the notes. See all my 18 observations on this date to get a full sense of the stand.

Disturbed lowland woods with a canopy of various native hardwoods, a serious invasion of Norway maple, and a typical understory composed of mostly invasive species like Privets, Burning Bush, and Multiflora Rose.

The southwest side of the loop has almost no native tree regeneration. There are some huge bitternut and shagbark hickories here, but almost every young tree growing here is a Norway maple. There are probably a couple hundred of them between 2-6" that would be great to remove at this stage. The northern section of the loop is dense with Ligustrum obtusifolium. Besides Carpinus carolinana and a few Viburnum prunifolium, a native understory is non-existent.

description:
A solo visit because I needed to get out somewhere, and I had not been to this very cool spot since May. I walked nearly the entire perimeter clockwise, except that I walked north along the powerline from the southern fenceline, then walked the remainder of the nature trail back to Jet. The entire route was about 4.8 miles. The weather at the start was overcast (at times sunny) and 62 degrees ("feels like" 62) with a light breeze. I left at 1359, after nearly 4 hours onsite.

I saw 10 Red-headed Woodpeckers and photographed 9 of them! Other  than Turkey Vultures overhead and a flock of 10 or more Pine Warblers along the southeastern edge, Red-headed Woodpeckers were the most common bird in the WEA today!

description:
This juvenile Coast Live Oak is growing next to Parking Lot I. It's 7-8 feet tall, potentially growing from a dead trunk.

It rained earlier today.

A well-known large clonal Palmer's Oak patch known as the "Jurupa Oak". 
 
It was discovered in the 1990's and has been determined to be at least 13,000 years old, making it probably the third oldest living plant of earth. A relic plant from the Pleistocene era.
 
Covering about 125 square meters, this plant is now threatened by encroaching development. Disjunct by almost 30 miles to others of the same species. 
 
Considering that tomorrow is New Year's Day, it was a good time to visit the plant and a good time to celebrate the plant - which has seen 13,000 "New Year's" in its life.

Happy New Year's Day!!!

description:
A thicket consisting of at least five Quercus garryana semota (shin oak) in close proximity. Some of the limbs were violently ripped out due to the intense flooding (or maybe snow avalanche? snow-induced flash flood?) in the winter storms last year which wiped out most of the plants on this hill (although they are now resprouting from their roots). 

Photos of growth habit, leaves of various shapes, acorn caps, and twigs. 

Several lichen were growing on the older bark. See here for the observations: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/196245212, https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/196245096

I almost thought that these were Rhus aromatica (which is also found here) until I saw the leaves. These are younger Quercus garryana semota. It seems that their original trunks were violently ripped out during the flooding/landslides (EDIT: okay, maybe not landslides. avalanche or flooding) that ensued during the winter storms last year. 

Don't worry—the caterpillar has a separate observation too: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/196247451

From a distance, the growth habit looked exactly like Q. garryana semota until I saw that it was semi-deciduous and had some green leaves. Upon closer look, the acorn caps and leaf outline were intermediate between Q. berberidifolia and QGS, and the buds looked like QGS but smaller. Acorn looks closer to Q. berberidifolia but still intermediate. Both Q. berberidifolia and QGS can be found in the vicinity.

Growing on a heavily disturbed hill (due to maybe snow avalanche? snow-induced flash flood? flash flooding due to other reasons?) with recovering interior chaparral.

Gall observation: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/196247779

In interior chaparral in northern Los Angeles County, shin oak is one of the only fully winter deciduous plants (and perhaps the only larger one). It is also the only one whose leaves are relatively large and turn a rich reddish-orange color before falling. Hence, during the winter months, thickets of shin oak can be found at a distance by looking for the following: 1) dense thickets of deciduous shrubs and 2) a bed of reddish-orange color underneath. Here, we can spot at least three thickets of shin oaks on the northern slopes of the ridge pictured.

-I'm leaning between White, Swamp White and Bur Oak as these white oak species are found in northern IL. 

- bark is silvery and flaky but these species do all have similar bark. 

-leaves are marcescent and I counted roughly 9 lobes. I'm leaning away from Bur Oak: they did not seem to be obovate (widest above middle of life) nor did they have a particularly deep pair of sinuses in the middle to form a 'waist'. As the leaves were last years and dried, I'm not sure how visible Swamp White Oak's classic strong contrast between green upper and white lower leaf surfaces would be.

-while I looked for acorns on the ground and found some, there was a variety of oak leaves (both white and red oaks) even right under the tree. So I didn't trust the acorns hadn't rolled or moved from a different tree. But there were definitely no Bur Oak acorns.

description:
*Quercus rubra* ("Red Oak"), Northern Red Oak

The most common of the Red Oaks found in Minnesota, Northern Red Oaks can be identified by: V-shaped sinuses with wide lobes, differentiating it from *Quercus ellipsoidalis*, Hill's/Northern Pin Oak and *Quercus coccinea*, Scarlet Oak, which have C-shaped sinuses and narrower lobes and also *Quercus palustris*, Southern Pin/Swamp Spanish Oak which can have U-shaped sinuses and also have narrower sinuses.
Their acorn caps are small, barely covering the base of the acorn, which distinguishes it from other Red Oak species present in the state.

Coast Live Oak (Quercus agrifolia) Native, long-lived tree (up to 125 - 250 years). Quercus agrifolia is by far the most common Oak tree on the Monterey Peninsula, CA. Leaves are evergreen, oval, cupped or spoon-shaped (adaxially convex). “Hairy armpits” at leaf veins on underside of Coast Live Oak leaf distinguishes it from other Quercus species. Margins of mature leaves have sharp spines that are very noticeable when you sit in the leaf litter. Acorns (fruits) are long and slender. There are 2 subspecies listed on Calflora.
Per Jepson eFlora: "Tree (6)10--25 m, evergreen; top wide; trunk bark furrowed, +- checkered, +- gray. Leaf: 2.5--6(9) cm; petiole 4--15 mm; blade generally widely elliptic to round, generally adaxially convex, +- dull green, abaxially glabrous to densely tomentose, dull, pale green, tip rounded to spine-toothed, margin rolled under or not, weakly spine-toothed. Fruit: cup 10--16 mm wide, 8--15 mm deep, obconic, scales thin, +- not tubercled, +- glabrous, +- brown; nut 25--35 mm, slender, ovoid, distally acute, shell woolly inside; mature in year 1. "

My favorite Coast Live Oak (Quercus agrifolia) observations:
Fruiting (acorns): https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/242561028

Coast Live Oak (Quercus agrifolia) A.k.a. CLO, is a native, long-lived tree (up to 125 - 250 years) in the High-latitude Oaks (Subgenus Quercus) and Beech (Fagaceae) family. Quercus agrifolia is by far the most common Oak tree on the Monterey Peninsula, CA. Leaves are evergreen, oval, cupped or spoon-shaped (adaxially convex). “Hairy armpits” at leaf veins on underside of CLO leaf distinguishes it from other Quercus species. Margins of mature leaves have sharp spines that are very noticeable when you sit in the leaf litter. Acorns (fruits) are long and slender.

Per Jepson eFlora: Coast Live Oak grows "(6)10--25 m, evergreen; top wide; trunk bark furrowed, +- checkered, +- gray. Leaf: 2.5--6(9) cm; petiole 4--15 mm; blade generally widely elliptic to round, generally adaxially convex, +- dull green, abaxially glabrous to densely tomentose, dull, pale green, tip rounded to spine-toothed, margin rolled under or not, weakly spine-toothed. Fruit: cup 10--16 mm wide, 8--15 mm deep, obconic, scales thin, +- not tubercled, +- glabrous, +- brown; nut 25--35 mm, slender, ovoid, distally acute, shell woolly inside; mature in year 1. "

Jepson eFlora https://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/eflora/eflora_display.php?tid=40530

Many organisms call CLO home. There is a whole INat project called "The wonderful diversity of life on Coast Live Oak" https://www.inaturalist.org/projects/the-wonderful-diversity-of-life-on-coast-live-oak. For example,

What causes those fuzzy, white "hairy armpits" where primary vein meets 2ndary veins? Answer: Mite Apartments. Per INat fredwatson: "the prevailing hypothesis is that they function as dolmatia - places for arthopods to live - in this case, mites. There's an idea that the mites either eat fungi or prey on herbivores that would otherwise damage the leaf. A 2020 paper by Coltharp et al. found support for the dolmatium hypothesis, but didn't find support for the predation or fungivory - perhaps because of small sample size and not necessarily because the process doesn't occur. So, mites live there, and there might be a benefit to the tree."

OAKs (genus Quercus) in general, have a worldwide distribution in Mediterranean climates.

Quercus (Oak) are in the Beech (Fagaceae) family.
Those found in Monterey County are in three groups: Red (or Black) Oaks, Intermediate Oaks, and White Oaks. Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks have acorns that generally mature over a 2 year period (Coast Live Oak is an exception to this rule). White Oaks have acorns that mature in a single season. Most Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks are evergreen (California Black Oak being the exception). White Oaks may be either evergreen or deciduous. Hybrid forms are common. All oaks are monoecious, with conspicuous male flowers. Female flowers are found in the axils of the leaves near the tips of the new stems.

description:
A solo visit to check on the Sparkleberry bushes. They're just starting to bloom, so the next 1-3 weeks should be great for hairstreaks. There were lots of lupines, pawpaws, and especially Lyreleaf Sages blooming. Butterflies were scarce but I photographed four species of moths. Variable Dancers were common; I quit photographing them after the 4th one encountered. I walked the usual trails in clockwise order, since I wanted to visit the main Sparkleberry patch first. I used my camera to take macro photographs, and after about 15 minutes of last using it, I realized that my phone was not in my pocket. I remembered where I last used it and back-tracked my path right to the phone.

Surprisingly, there were few vehicles in the parking lot at my arrival, and no mother truckers on the mound. (Did somebody from FWC or SWFWMD finally tell the mother truckers that a state preserve is not appropriate for them to run their r/c vehicles over the area?). Several people were crossing Aripeka Road to go swimming in the pond to the south. 

The weather at my arrival was sunny and 79 degrees ("feels like" 82) -- both temperatures seemed low -- with a light breeze. The weather when I left was one degree warmer, which again seemed too low. I left at 1717 after exactly 3 hours and headed home.

Blue Oak (Quercus douglasii) Endemic to California. A.k.a. Blue, white, mountain, rock, iron, post, jack, and Douglas Oak. OAKs (genus Quercus) in general:

Quercus (Oak) are in the Beech (Fagaceae) family.
Those found in Monterey County are in three groups: Red (or Black) Oaks, Intermediate Oaks, and White Oaks. Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks have acorns that generally mature over a 2 year period (Coast Live Oak is an exception to this rule). White Oaks have acorns that mature in a single season. Most Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks are evergreen (California Black Oak being the exception). White Oaks may be either evergreen or deciduous. Hybrid forms are common. All oaks are monoecious, with conspicuous male flowers. Female flowers are found in the axils of the leaves near the tips of the new stems.

description: On 10/3/74 [James Griffin vouchered a discovery of *Quercus palmeri*](https://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/new_detail?PGM1704&YF=0) in the Clear Creek area of San Benito County. At that time this was a new, isolated, northerly station for this unusual species. Griiffin returned about 3 weeks later with his botanist friend and CA oak maven John Tucker, and together they collected a number of additional vouchers. At that time *Q. palmeri* went by the name *Q. dunni* (after the remarkable late-1800's naturalist & collector George Dunn, see Jepson's brief bio here). Later Griffin & Tucker published a 1976 Madroño note on the newly discovered station. Motivated by the above, and a prior interest in this species, I was eager to look for these Palmer Oaks...and joined Joyce Gross & Alice Abela to search for them, almost 50 years after Griffin & Tucker's voucher collections. After planning and walking a route with a number of promising point locations suggested by the Madroño note & voucher labels, we seemed to have struck-out on our "best candidate sites" and were becoming somewhat discouraged. But crossing a creek after the road we were on faded out, Joyce came upon a smaller trail following the SW side of the creek, and within a few hundred feet there were 3 or 4 clumps of Palmer Oaks growing on the steep bank above the trail :-). Note that zooming-in on the iNat inset map above, the observation icon appears to the NE of the trail shown there...but that's an artifact of errors in either my camera's GPS reading, the rendering of the trail on the map, or both. The rough location is correct, but the trail follows the SW side of the creek there...and the Palmer Oaks are rooted along the eroding upper edge of the tall bank just SW of the trail. Palmer Oak is thought to be a relict species that had a more widespread and continuous distribution in Pleistocene and Pliocene times. Except for a few areas in southern California, northern Baja California, and Arizona (see SEINet map here), nowadays it is usually found in small isolated stands of a few individuals, which are often clonal groupings...and these stands are typically many miles apart (e.g. ten, twenty, or much more!). One particular clonal colony growing high on a granitic summit in the Jurupa Hills of Riverside County, CA has been estimated to be 13,000+ years old in this 2009 paper. The plants here were growing in 3 or 4 "clumps" of scrub to small tree-like stature — each with one to several small, clustered, multiple trunks. They appeared less clonal in growth form than other Palmer Oak groupings I've seen...but may have been clonal. I have no idea how old these plants currently are, but they may have difficulty persisting for a truly long time into the future at this site — as their roots are being undercut by erosion of the bank above the old jeep road/trail and adjacent creek. This may be exacerbated in part by human impacts...recent motorcycle tracks were apparent, and a large branch had been cut off and was lying by the trail (visible in 8th photo above, at center left). Some branches were overhanging the trail...and Palmer Oaks are notoriously rigidly-branched with leaves that are viciously stiff & spine-margined! Wouldn't want to hit a branch, or even of a spray of twigs, while speeding past. In addition to the Jepson eFlora treatment for *Q. palmeri*, more info is available on the SEINet page here.

I walked the southern nature trail to the powerlines, then walked north, then circled the burn clockwise. I returned to the nature trail and took it back to Jet. All duplicate species -- including the grasshoppers, the buckeyes, and the swallowtails -- represent different individuals; grasshoppers were abundant on the sandy road under the powerlines. description:
With Don Fraser; a visit to see what was around -- the trip quickly turned into a contest to see how many yucca moths we could find. We checked every Common Yucca that we found; some were not yet blooming, but we ended up with 17 blooming yuccas out of 17 with yucca moths! It was amazing! By my count, I photographed at least 49 moths! The weather at the start (1030) was overcast with brief, light rain and 75 degrees. By the end (1453), it was sunny, and about 90 degrees.

Photographs taken with my cell phone (Samsung Galaxy A52) have precise locations. Photographs taken with my camera (Panasonic Lumix FZ80) have a generic location. We iNatted five locations -- in addition to the sites around every blooming Common Yucca that we found -- with the most time at any single site spent at the heliport near Bald Eagle Nest Sink near the southern end of South Road. We were north of Rattlesnake Camp Road only for our final ~75 minutes, when we drove Gopher Road adjacent to US-19, north to the Hernando Sportsmen's Club gate.
